hook: Warm ocean pulses are quietly raising sea levels along the shoreline.

sections.voiceover: Warm ocean pulses are quietly raising sea levels along the shoreline.
sections.visual_cue: Cinematic slow-motion shot of ocean waves crashing along a steep rocky shoreline.

sections.voiceover: In October 2026, trapped Kelvin waves moved north along the U.S. West Coast. These surges mark an early sign of a Super El Niño. How high will water rise along the Pacific Ocean?
sections.visual_cue: Satellite ocean graphic tracking warm water pulse anomalies advancing northward along the coast.
b_roll: U.S. West Coast shoreline map overlay

sections.voiceover: NOAA tracked similar coastally trapped Kelvin waves during the 1997/1998 El Niño event last century.
sections.visual_cue: Archival ocean indicators data graphic showing sea surface height anomalies along the Pacific shoreline.
b_roll: NOAA sea level anomaly chart animation
Ocean monitoring buoy floating on waves

sections.voiceover: Sea levels along the U.S. West Coast rose by up to 1 foot in October 2026. Measurements tracked daily anomalies relative to the 1993 to 2012 baseline average. The warm surge alters coastal water heights.
sections.visual_cue: Data visualization depicting sea level rise measurements peaking up to 1 foot above baseline.
b_roll: High tide coastal water creeping up shoreline

sections.voiceover: Coastal waters remain elevated as waves travel further north.
sections.visual_cue: Wide cinematic sunset shot of the Pacific ocean horizon with rolling waves.
b_roll: Waves moving northward along Pacific coast
